title: Adaptive fidelity routing heuristics for overload resilience
body:
Goal and context:
This is a working note for an approach we are calling 'adaptive fidelity routing' — a control-plane + routing policy pattern intended to keep end-user latency and availability stable under constrained capacity without doing hard capacity preemption. Instead of bluntly cutting traffic or switching to a single hard-fallback model, the system moves requests along a graded fidelity ladder (smaller/cheaper model, reduced context, truncated generation, cached/approximate responses) according to clear signals.

Why this differs from prior approaches:
- Emphasis on preserving perceived functionality rather than preserving a specific model.
- Fine-grained, reversible interventions (fidelity changes) at per-request level instead of global hard redirects.
- Control plane expresses policies as layered primitives (fidelity bands, cost/latency budgets, routing predicates) that region agents enforce.

Key concepts and vocabulary (short):
- Fidelity band: a named configuration for request handling (e.g., fidelity:premium, fidelity:standard, fidelity:fast). Each band maps to a model variant, generation constraints, and optional feature flags.
- Fidelity ladder: ordered list of bands from highest quality to most approximate.
- Regional agent: lightweight local controller in each region that applies policy decisions using local telemetry and global guardrails.
- Hedging window: a short timeout for starting a cheaper speculative response while waiting for premium path.
- Prefix-eviction budget: budget that controls how aggressively we use prefix/KV caches to serve degraded responses.

Fidelity bands (example mappings):
- premium: large-uniquantized model, full context, beam sampling, support for tool-calls and function-calling enabled.
- standard: medium-size quantized variant, full context up to 2048 tokens, no beams, deterministic decoding preferred.
- fast: small low-latency variant, context window 1024, strict max tokens, sampling with higher temperature for speed.
- concise-cache: generate summary from prefix cache / use retrieval-augmented short response, no external tool calls.

Routing primitives and predicates:
- latency_p50/p95/p99 thresholds per route and customer tier.
- queue_depth (number of inflight requests queued for runtime).
- GPU_util and GPU_queue_seconds.
- recent_slo_violation_rate (5m window).
- cache_hit_rate for prefix/KV cache.

Example policy (human-readable):
1) Try premium band target if p95_latency < 350ms AND gpu_util < 70% AND queue_depth < 40.
2) If p95_latency in [350ms, 600ms] OR gpu_util in [70%, 85%], route to premium but also schedule a hedging speculative request to fast band at t=150ms. Whichever returns first wins; the other is canceled if possible.
3) If p95_latency > 600ms OR recent_slo_violation_rate > 1% OR queue_depth > 200, short-circuit to standard band. If cache_hit_rate > 0.15 for route, prefer concise-cache.
4) If outage detected (regional agent reports unacceptable node failures) then move all non-SLA traffic to concise-cache and only allow premium for whitelisted customers.

Control-plane responsibilities and interfaces:
- Global policy store: stores band definitions, rollout weights, per-tenant overrides, hedging timeouts.
- Region agents: subscribe to policy diffs and push local decisions to edge routing layer. Must operate autonomously for up to 5 minutes without control-plane contact.
- Tagging: requests carry stability tags (customer_tier, session_affinity, model_hints) used to evaluate predicates.
- Observability hooks: every decision must emit decision_reason and applied_band.

Multi-region considerations:
- Proactive cross-region reroute: when region_util > 80% and estimated cross-region latency penalty < configured SLA delta, region agent can forward to partner region following bandwidth/egress budget rules.
- Session affinity and KV cache boundary: prefer to keep sessions in same region for KV cache locality; if crossing regions, invalidate or fall back to concise-cache for first few requests.
- Staggered degradation: orchestrate a sequencing where non-interactive routes degrade first (batch jobs, long-running inferences) then interactive non-critical, then critical interactive.

Telemetry & SLOs to monitor (minimum set):
- per-route p50/p95/p99 token latency (by band)
- per-route applied_band distribution (percentage of requests served in each band)
- hedging_win_rate (how often the hedged speculative request wins)
- per-tenant error rates and token-cost-per-request (by band)
- cache_fidelity_delta (percent of times concise-cache returns acceptable result vs premium in a random sample)
- regional_utilization and cross-region-egress usage

Operational playbook (short):
- Trigger A (early warning): p95 crossing first threshold for 10m -> region agent enters "soft-fidelity-mode": increase fast band probability by 20%, enable hedging for premium with 150ms window. Notify on-call.
- Trigger B (sustained pressure): p95 > high threshold for 3m OR gpu_util sustained above 85% -> region agent switches to "strict-fidelity-mode": route non-SLA to standard/concise-cache; block new premium sessions beyond concurrency cap.
- Trigger C (partial outage): node group failing -> route to partner region if cross-region budget available; if not, escalate to manual operator to initiate capacity scale or preemptive evictions.
- Manual overrides: must include a reason, expected duration, and rollback instructions. UI shows impacted routes and % of traffic shifted.

Experiments and heuristics we've tried (short journal):
- Synthetic spike test: 3x traffic for 15m to single region. Result: hedging + small fast-band produced 1.4x lower p99 compared to immediate global redirect, and UX complaints in user panel dropped by 18%.
- Cache-first approach: enabling concise-cache for long-tail queries reduced token costs by 26% but increased mismatches (semantic quality) by ~3% in a sampled evaluation. Good for low-risk routes.
- Session-weighted routing: pinning premium band for first N requests of a session improved retention for pro customers; degrade after N=5 requests reduced costs without increased complaint volume.

Risk and failure modes:
- Quality cliffs: too aggressive switching to small models can produce hallucination regressions for certain prompt families. Need per-route quality monitoring and automatic rollback on regression.
- Cache staleness / correctness: concise-cache may surface stale context when cross-region or when session writes occur. Clear rules: read-only cache acceptable, otherwise fall back to standard band.
- Billing surprises: hedging increases total tokens if both speculative and premium run concurrently and both finish. Use cancellation hooks aggressively and set hedging only where expected win-rate justifies cost.

Open questions / next steps (actionable):
- Define a canonical fidelity-band schema and store it in the policy proto (TODO: pick fields and serialization).
- Implement a small region-agent prototype that can simulate a 5-minute control-plane outage and still make decisions.
- Experiment: run A/B with hedging window 100/150/200ms on two customer cohorts to measure hedging win-rate vs cost.
- Build a lightweight regression detector that ties to eval prompts to surface quality regressions caused by band transitions.

References and quick links:
- Notes: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/PLAT/Adaptive+Fidelity+Notes
- Related proposal: https://github.com/redwood-inference/routing-proto/pull/142
- Jira prototype epic: JIRA-PLAT-834

Short conclusion: adaptive-fidelity routing gives us a middle path between complete spillover and single fallback redirects. It requires discipline in observability and careful per-route tuning but can reduce user-visible outages and control token-costs more smoothly. This doc is a working draft — aiming to get feedback from SRE, serving-runtime, and product routing owners before we standardize band schema and start implementation.
